name: ATP6V0A2-CDG (autosomal recessive cutis laxa type IIA)

clinicalPearls: ATP6V0A2 encodes the a2 subunit of the membrane-embedded V0 domain of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, which acidifies the Golgi and endosomal compartments; its loss impairs both glycosylation and elastic-fibre formation.
It is a combined N- and O-glycosylation disorder, so both serum transferrin (N-glycan) and apolipoprotein C-III (mucin-type O-glycan) isoform patterns are typically abnormal.
The gene underlies both autosomal recessive cutis laxa type IIA and the allelic wrinkly skin syndrome, which form a phenotypic continuum.
The skin is loose, redundant and wrinkled, most obvious over the face, abdomen and hands, and may partially improve with age.
A large, late-closing anterior fontanelle, downslanting palpebral fissures and a long philtrum are characteristic dysmorphic clues.
Neurological involvement with developmental delay and seizures is common, and neuronal migration abnormalities such as a cobblestone-like malformation may be seen on imaging.
Skeletal features include joint laxity, hip dislocation and delayed bone age, and strabismus and myopia are frequent.
reference.pathophysiology: The vacuolar H+-ATPase maintains the acidic luminal pH of the Golgi apparatus and the endosomal-lysosomal system. ATP6V0A2 encodes an isoform of the membrane-embedded a subunit of the proton-translocating V0 domain that is important for Golgi acidification and vesicular trafficking. When it is deficient, defective luminal acidification perturbs the activity and localisation of pH-sensitive glycosyltransferases and glycosidases, producing a combined defect of N-linked and mucin-type O-linked glycosylation. Disturbed Golgi trafficking also impairs secretion and assembly of tropoelastin and processing of elastic-fibre components, leaving the dermis with sparse, fragmented elastic fibres and giving the cutis laxa phenotype, while hypoglycosylation of numerous other proteins accounts for the neurological, skeletal and connective-tissue manifestations. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited cutis laxa syndromes (ELN, EFEMP2/FBLN4, FBLN5, LTBP4)
De Barsy syndrome and related PYCR1 or ALDH18A1 disorders
Other combined N- and O-glycosylation CDGs such as COG-complex defects
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and other heritable connective-tissue disorders
Menkes disease and occipital horn syndrome (ATP7A)
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing (a type II pattern)
Apolipoprotein C-III isoform analysis as an O-glycosylation screen
Skin biopsy with elastic-fibre staining showing fragmented or reduced fibres
Neuroimaging for cortical malformation and migration defects
Ophthalmological review for strabismus and myopia
redFlags: Seizures accompanied by a structural neuronal migration abnormality
Complications of connective-tissue fragility such as hernias
Feeding difficulty and growth failure in infancy
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is often relatively preserved and the cutaneous laxity may improve with age, but neurodevelopmental outcome varies and can include lasting cognitive and motor impairment.
pitfalls: Testing only N-glycosylation with transferrin and missing the disorder, as O-glycosylation screening with apolipoprotein C-III is also needed
Attributing cutis laxa to a purely dermatological or connective-tissue cause without metabolic screening
Overlooking a structural brain malformation as the cause of seizures
Confusing it with elastin-related or De Barsy syndrome cutis laxa
references: Congenital disorders of glycosylation review literature
management: Provide supportive care as there is no disease-specific therapy, protecting the fragile lax skin and reserving plastic surgical correction for functionally or cosmetically significant redundancy, recognising it may recur
Support neurodevelopment with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy and individualised educational provision
Manage seizures with anticonvulsant therapy guided by neurology
Optimise feeding and nutrition and monitor growth in infancy and childhood
Undertake surveillance for connective-tissue and vascular complications, including herniae and arterial tortuosity, alongside ophthalmic and skeletal review
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through metabolic medicine, neurology and clinical genetics, and offer genetic counselling with family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
